flashcards.q: Describe price-time priority matching and three order types that encode execution intent.
flashcards.a: Resting orders queue FIFO at each price level; marketable orders sweep levels best-first. Types: limit (price-capped, rests if unmarketable), IOC/FOK (immediate-or-cancel / fill-or-kill), iceberg (display a slice, hide residual to reduce information leakage), pegged/midpoint (track NBBO).

flashcards.q: Decompose the bid-ask spread into its three economic components.
flashcards.a: (1) Order-processing costs (smallest, per-share fixed). (2) Inventory-risk compensation (maker holds position until offset; scales with volatility). (3) Adverse-selection cost - expected loss to informed counterparties (Glosten-Milgrom: spreads exist even with zero costs and risk-neutral makers purely from information asymmetry).

flashcards.q: Derive Roll's effective-spread estimator from serial covariance of price changes.
flashcards.a: p_t = m_t + (s/2)*q_t with q_t = +/-1 trade direction and random-walk mid. Then cov(dp_t, dp_{t-1}) = -(s/2)^2 because the bounce anticorrelates adjacent changes. s_hat = 2*sqrt(-cov_hat) when covariance negative. Fails on trending prices; superseded by Corwin-Schultz/Hasbrouck-Gibbs where tape data is unavailable.

flashcards.q: State the square-root law with typical coefficients (marked ~) and why sqrt scaling emerges.
flashcards.a: dp ~ Y * sigma_daily * sqrt(Q/VADV), Y ~ 0.4-1.0 marked ~ (Almgren et al 2005; Tóth et al universality across asset classes). Sqrt emerges from diffusion of metaorder information through liquidity providers - cumulative impact grows like sqrt(t) during execution. Doubling size adds only ~41% cost.

flashcards.q: Temporary vs permanent impact: define both and their P&L consequences.
flashcards.a: Temporary = liquidity consumption that reverts after execution ends - pure cost of speed, avoidable by slowing down. Permanent = information conveyed; price ratchets permanently - unavoidable by scheduling, only by trading less or hiding better. Almgren-Chriss minimize permanent+temporary cost plus lambda-weighted timing variance.

flashcards.q: Give the maker/taker economics and the maker's core risk.
flashcards.a: Maker earns spread + rebate (~+0.2bp typical credit) IF filled, bearing queue-position risk AND adverse selection (fills arrive because informed flow hit your quote - winner's curse). Taker pays half-spread + fee (~0.35bp) for certainty. PFOF exists because retail flow is uninformed: wholesalers internalize profitably even after price improvement.

flashcards.q: Your resting limit buy fills. Why is this conditionally bad news?
flashcards.a: You were filled BECAUSE someone chose to trade against you: either noise (fine - spread earned) or informed flow (you just bought before down-drift). Expected fill quality = spread capture minus adverse-selection rent; markouts confirm passive fills systematically underperform prevailing mid. Profitable making requires neutral flow or toxicity-detection/skewing tech.

flashcards.q: List the five fill fantasies that make backtests overstate performance.
flashcards.a: (1) Mid-price fills save half-spread both sides. (2) Infinite queue priority on passive fills. (3) No adverse selection conditional on filling. (4) Zero latency drift between signal and execution. (5) No self-impact/capacity constraint. Aggregate damage commonly 30-80% of gross Sharpe (marked ~) - hence TCA desks and tier-3/4 backtest simulation.

flashcards.q: What does an implementation-shortfall algo optimize beyond VWAP/TWAP?
flashcards.a: The Almgren-Chriss frontier: schedule trades to minimize impact cost plus lambda-weighted timing-risk variance of remaining inventory. Front-load when alpha decays fast or risk aversion low; back-load when impact dominates. VWAP tracks volume but ignores YOUR alpha profile and risk aversion - right only for benchmark mandates.

flashcards.q: Define implementation shortfall decomposition and markout analysis.
flashcards.a: IS: parent-order slippage vs arrival price decomposed into delay cost + execution cost + opportunity cost of unfilled remainder (Perold 1988 benchmark). Markouts: post-fill drift at +1s/+1min/+1h vs YOUR fill price - buys drifting down after fills means you overpaid; isolates execution quality from strategy quality.

flashcards.q: Key US structure numbers: venues, off-exchange share, latency arms race.
flashcards.a: ~16 registered exchanges + 30-40 ATSs/dark pools under Reg NMS ($0.01 tick); ~42-47% of US equity volume executes off-exchange (dark pools + internalizing wholesalers). Latency: microwave NYC-Chicago one-way ~4ms vs fiber ~7ms+; IEX sells a deliberate 350-microsecond speed bump. Close auctions print ~10%+ of daily volume.

flashcards.q: What problem does Avellaneda-Stoikov solve and what is the reservation price?
flashcards.a: Optimal market-making quotes under inventory risk: reservation (indifference) mid shifts AWAY from fair value proportional to current inventory and risk aversion - long inventory quotes lower bid/higher ask skew to attract sells. Assumes stationary arrivals/diffusion; breaks in flash crashes when cancellations explode and arrivals become one-sided - survivors run hard inventory caps and auto-widen triggers.

flashcards.q: Tradeoffs of dark-pool aggregation versus lit sweeps for a large parent order.
flashcards.a: Dark: midpoint matching saves half-spread (~1-2bp), hides intent, but faces toxic counterparties, reduced fill probability per ping, and ATS volume-threshold rules post-2016. Lit: immediate NBBO-protected liquidity but displays intent inviting front-running and pre-impact. Production answer: passive-dark-first patient slices, lit postings inside spread opportunistically, lit sweeps under deadline pressure, venue TCA adjusting mix monthly.

flashcards.q: Why do closing auctions print 10%+ of US equity volume and what makes auction fills special?
flashcards.a: Passive/index rebalancing benchmarks to closing prints so natural flow concentrates there; single-price uniform clearing removes queue/spread/urgency costs - minimal impact per share. Pre-close imbalance messages reveal net supply/demand (also leaking participant interest). Catches: close-benchmark concentration, marking-the-close enforcement risk, execution metric set by the very flow you add.
